name: Columnar Formats and Partitioning
intent: Lay analytical data out so a query reads only the partitions, row groups and columns it needs, instead of scanning the whole table.
scenario: A click-events table holds 30 days at 400,000 rows a day, stored as 138-byte rows. An analyst asks for user_id, country and amount for the last 7 days where amount is at least 900. Stored as row files the query reads all 30 days, every column; stored as day-partitioned columnar files it reads a few percent of that.
problem: Analytical queries touch a few columns of a few billion rows, while row-oriented storage (CSV, JSON, Avro) forces the reader to fetch and parse every column of every row, including a 120-byte payload nobody asked for. Object storage charges and waits per byte and per request, so scanning everything makes queries slow and expensive, and nothing in a pile of files tells the engine which ones can be ignored.

howItWorks.title: Store each column contiguously, in row groups
howItWorks.text: A columnar file such as Parquet or ORC splits rows into row groups (commonly 128 MB to 1 GB of data, or roughly 100,000 to a few million rows) and, inside a group, writes one column chunk per column. A query that needs 3 of 40 columns reads only those chunks. Values of one type sit next to each other, so they compress far better than mixed rows.

howItWorks.title: Encode and compress each chunk by its data
howItWorks.text: Low-cardinality columns use dictionary encoding (each distinct string stored once, rows hold small integer codes), repeated runs use run-length encoding, and integers use bit-packing or delta encoding, then a general codec like Snappy or Zstd is applied on top. Typical analytical tables shrink 3x to 10x against CSV, but a column of random strings or already-compressed blobs barely shrinks.

howItWorks.title: Keep statistics in the footer
howItWorks.text: The file ends with a footer holding the schema and, for every column chunk, its offset, row count and min/max (plus null count, and optionally a Bloom filter). A reader fetches the footer first, with one ranged read of the file tail, then decides which chunks to fetch. A row group whose amount max is 640 cannot contain amount >= 900, so none of its bytes are read. This only works when values are clustered: if every group spans 0 to 999, nothing can be skipped.

howItWorks.title: Partition the directory layout by a low-cardinality key
howItWorks.text: Files are written under paths such as events/day=2026-10-04/part-0007.parquet. A filter on day lets the planner drop whole directories using only the path, without opening a file. Hive-style partitions are the convention, and table formats such as Iceberg and Delta track partitions in metadata instead of by listing directories.

howItWorks.title: Pick partition keys, sort order and file size together
howItWorks.text: Partition on what queries nearly always filter by (usually event date) and keep it to hundreds or thousands of partitions, not millions. Inside a partition, sort or cluster by the next most selective column so min/max statistics prune, and compact files toward 128 MB to 1 GB each: thousands of tiny files cost more in listing, opening and footer reads than in bytes.

pros: Reads only the needed columns, so scans of wide tables touch a small fraction of the bytes
Per-column encoding and compression typically shrink data 3x to 10x against CSV or JSON
Partition pruning and min/max statistics skip whole directories and row groups before any data is read
Self-describing: the footer carries the schema and statistics, and the formats are read by Spark, Trino, DuckDB, BigQuery, Snowflake and others
cons: Poor for point lookups and for fetching whole rows, because one row is spread across every column chunk
Files are immutable: updates and deletes mean rewriting files or layering a table format on top
Writes are batched and memory-hungry, since a row group is buffered and encoded in memory before it is flushed
Layout choices (partition key, sort order, file size) are decided at write time and are costly to change later
whenToUse: Analytical scans and aggregations over large tables where queries select a handful of columns
Data lakes and warehouses on object storage, where bytes read and requests made are the cost
Data that is written once in batches and read many times, with a date or similar key in most filters
whenNotToUse: Transactional workloads, key lookups and row-at-a-time updates, which belong in a row store or LSM/B-tree database
Small tables (a few hundred MB or less): a single CSV or a database table scans fast enough and partitioning only adds files
Streaming sinks that must be queryable within seconds, unless a table format or compaction handles the small files they produce
Partitioning by a high-cardinality key such as user_id, which creates millions of tiny directories
pitfalls: The small-files problem: streaming or over-parallel writers emit thousands of files of a few MB each, so listing, opening and reading footers dominates query time; compact them
Over-partitioning (by user_id or by hour on a tiny table) creates millions of partitions, slow listings and a bloated catalog
Data skew: one hot partition (a null key, a default country, one huge customer) holds most of the data and makes a single task the straggler
Statistics that cannot prune because the data is not clustered: filtering on a column whose every row group spans the full range still reads everything unless you sort or Z-order on write
Filtering by a function of the partition column (for example WHERE date_trunc('week', ts) = ...) or comparing it with a mismatched type can defeat pruning; filter on the partition column itself
Changing the partition scheme or schema later requires rewriting the data, so check schema-evolution rules before adding or renaming columns

roles.label: Query engine
roles.description: Plans the query, prunes partitions and row groups, and fetches only the column chunks it needs.

roles.label: Partition layout
roles.description: The directory structure (day=...) that lets the planner discard whole days from the path alone.

roles.label: File footer
roles.description: Schema plus per-row-group, per-column min/max statistics, read before any data.

roles.label: Column chunks
roles.description: Encoded, compressed values of one column for one row group, fetched with ranged reads.
